Three moves for Indegene across these six accounts.

Four products are launching or awaiting a dated decision, four of these six companies are under a public savings commitment, and five are carrying an event that has to be communicated carefully. Each opens a different door — this issue shows which one to knock on, and where.

Three plays for this quarter

01

Launches with a decision already dated: be in place before it

What’s happeningRoche has Susvimo approved in the EU and paediatric Ocrevus through CHMP. Takeda has ORZEYFUL approved in both the US and Japan, MIMRYLO approved in polycythemia vera, and zasocitinib under Priority Review to a Q1 2027 target. Boehringer is scaling JASCAYD and HERNEXEOS behind 20% Human Pharma growth.
What to doWork back from each approval or decision date and open the conversation 60–90 days ahead: payer and HEOR evidence, medical and field enablement, and patient-support operations. Where the label changes how treatment is delivered rather than what is said about it, lead with the operating model — site workflow, scheduling, refill logistics — not the campaign.
Why nowSusvimo turns monthly eye injections into roughly two refills a year, and ORZEYFUL treats a disease most patients wait years to have named. Neither is a messaging problem. Both are operations problems, and operations get decided early.

02

Cost and price pressure: lead with what the work replaces

What’s happeningCSL has posted a US$2.6B statutory loss and agreed international-comparable Medicaid pricing with HHS. Germany's fixed 8.5% supplementary discount is now law, taking patented-drug rebates to 15.5%, and has already cost Boehringer a €900M investment decision. Takeda is running a transformation programme targeting over JPY 200bn in annualised savings, and Sanofi is moving 20 mature medicines and three plants to Cheplapharm.
What to doPrice every proposal as cost-to-serve. Show what comes off the client's own cost base — content and MLR throughput, channel consolidation, work moved out of in-house teams — and attach a measured outcome to each. Put the number in the first page, not the appendix.
Why nowIn four of these six accounts the budget holder has made a savings commitment in public. This year a capability pitch loses to a cost case, however good the capability.

Roche
ACT NOW

Window  Susvimo EU launch open; three readouts in one week

NUDGE’s read

Roche has moved from pipeline to portfolio in motion. The EU approval of Susvimo is the one with immediate operational consequence: a refillable implant that cuts treatment to roughly twice a year rewrites clinic scheduling, refill logistics and the payer model, not just the message. Behind it sit three readouts inside one week — sefaxersen in IgA nephropathy, paediatric Ocrevus at CHMP, and Lunsumio in follicular lymphoma — plus two discovery deals and a new Boston centre pointing the company at cardio-renal-metabolic disease and AI-designed chemistry. The nomination of a former Takeda CEO to the board signals commercial discipline arriving at the top.

What Indegene should do

1Susvimo EU launch operations — country-by-country HTA and payer evidence, treatment-pattern analytics showing the shift from monthly injections to twice-yearly refills, and the clinic workflow and refill scheduling that ophthalmology units have to design before the first patients are implanted.
2Sefaxersen and paediatric Ocrevus launch readiness — nephrology and paediatric-neurology field enablement, regulatory and medical communications, and the evidence packages both assets need while the filings are still in flight rather than after approval.
3CVRM and AI data operations — position against the Boston centre and the Atavistik and Dualitas collaborations: congress and publication planning, plus the data governance and model-management discipline that AI-designed discovery creates and that regulators will eventually ask about.

CSL
ACT NOW

Window  Reset year after a US$2.6B loss; AWS build under way

NUDGE’s read

CSL is in a declared reset. A US$2.6B statutory loss on US$7.1B of impairments, a board publicly acknowledging shareholder frustration and saying it is acting with urgency, and investment narrowing towards plasma — every proposal this year is read against cost to serve rather than capability. Two openings are live and neither depends on new spend. The US government agreements create pricing, reporting and onshoring work with deadlines already attached, and ANDEMBRY's Canadian reimbursement expansion is an access launch happening now. And as of 29 September it has an AWS collaboration running across research data, clinical development, protocol authoring, regulatory submissions and governance — CSL is building capability in exactly the workflows an outside partner would otherwise sell it, so scope the work around that build rather than across it.

What Indegene should do

1Rebuild open proposals as cost-to-serve — recast everything in flight around unit cost and measured outcome: content and MLR throughput, channel consolidation, and work that moves off CSL's own cost base. Lead with what the engagement replaces, not what it adds.
2US pricing and onshoring work stream — Medicaid pricing analytics and reporting against the HHS agreement, plus the regulatory, employee and policy communications the $1.5B Kankakee expansion generates over the next two years.
3ANDEMBRY Canada access execution — payer materials, HCP outreach and patient-support operations for the newly funded provinces and federal plans, while the access decision is fresh and prescribing patterns are still forming.

Takeda
ACT NOW

Window  Two approvals launching; zasocitinib decision targeted Q1 2027

NUDGE’s read

Takeda has three launches running at once and a fourth decision already dated. ORZEYFUL is approved in both the US and Japan for narcolepsy type 1 — the first treatment aimed at the orexin deficiency behind the disease, in a population that typically waits years for a diagnosis and sits with sleep specialists and neurologists who have to be found before they can be reached. MIMRYLO adds polycythemia vera, partnered with Protagonist. Zasocitinib is under Priority Review with a Q1 2027 target, which means the dermatology launch has to be built now. All of it runs against a transformation programme targeting over JPY 200bn in annualised savings, so every proposal has to arrive costed.

What Indegene should do

1Rare-disease patient finding for ORZEYFUL — narcolepsy type 1 diagnosis runs years behind symptom onset. Map the sleep-medicine and neurology referral pathway across the US and Japan, build the diagnosis and treatment education behind it, and run the patient-support operations that turn an approval into treated patients.
2Zasocitinib dermatology launch readiness — payer evidence, field enablement and medical content built to the Q1 2027 target date rather than assembled after it, with the EMA filing running in parallel and a second market to plan for.
3MIMRYLO haematology launch with Protagonist — co-promotion governance, haematologist education and patient support for a first-in-class hepcidin mimetic — partnered launches fail on coordination far more often than on evidence.

Sanofi
ACT NOW

Window  20 medicines moving to Cheplapharm; two live supply failures

NUDGE’s read

Sanofi is growing and simplifying at the same time, and both create work. Full-year guidance is up to around 10% growth, while 20 mature medicines and three manufacturing sites move to Cheplapharm from Q1 2027 — a divestment that has to be explained to prescribers, pharmacists and payers in every affected market without disrupting supply. Against that, two supply failures are already live: Pompe medicines short after an FDA manufacturing citation, and the England flu vaccine short before the autumn campaign. And the European Commission has a formal antitrust investigation open into whether Sanofi disparaged a rival flu vaccine. Supply and conduct are the same conversation here — what gets said, to whom, with what approval trail behind it.

What Indegene should do

1Cheplapharm transition communications — prescriber, pharmacist and payer notification across every affected market as 20 medicines and three sites change hands, with the labelling and regulatory updates that follow. This is country-by-country work with a fixed start date and no natural owner inside either company.
2Supply-disruption communications as a standing capability — the Pompe shortage and the England flu gap both need clinician and patient communications that are compliant, fast and consistent across markets. Pre-agree the playbook and the approval route rather than rebuilding both under time pressure at the next event.
3Promotional governance and MLR discipline — with a formal EC investigation into vaccine-campaign conduct open, every claim, channel and approval record is potential evidence. Offer review, audit and traceability operations — not additional campaign volume.

Novartis
BUILD

Window  Two Phase III misses and one win in a single month

NUDGE’s read

Novartis's September was two failures and one success, and that changes where the work sits. Pelacarsen missed its primary endpoint in Lp(a)HORIZON and del-desiran missed in myotonic dystrophy — the latter an asset from the $12B Avidity acquisition, so expect scrutiny of what that platform delivers next. Remibrutinib succeeded in two Phase III relapsing MS trials: an oral BTK inhibitor entering a crowded market where positioning against established orals and infusions is the entire contest. Canada's Vanrafia decision shows the access bar the company is now applying country by country — it withdrew from the reimbursement path on an already-approved drug.

What Indegene should do

1Remibrutinib MS launch positioning — the differentiation case against established oral and infused therapies: comparative and real-world evidence, neurologist education, and payer submissions prepared while the filings are being assembled rather than after the label lands.
2Communications for the failed readouts — pelacarsen and del-desiran both need investigator, patient and payer communications plus trial wind-down operations. It is time-bound, unglamorous work that is usually unowned, which is exactly why it is worth offering.
3Country-level access strategy — the Vanrafia withdrawal was a judgement about the Canadian access environment, not about the asset. Offer the HTA and pricing analytics that decide which markets are worth filing in before the submission spend is committed.

Boehringer Ingelheim
BUILD

Window  20% Human Pharma growth; German rebate now 15.5%

NUDGE’s read

Boehringer is growing hard and buying AI capability while fighting its home market on price. First-half sales reached €15.8B, up 16.2%, with Human Pharma up 20.1% on JARDIANCE and the JASCAYD and HERNEXEOS launches. Inside a single month it licensed Owkin's AI platform and committed up to $1B to Envisagenics for solid-tumour targets identified from RNA splicing. At the same time Germany's fixed 8.5% supplementary discount is now law, taking patented-drug rebates to 15.5%, and Boehringer has already cancelled €900M of planned German investment over it. Growth funds the launches; the German margin decides how they get resourced.

What Indegene should do

1JASCAYD and HERNEXEOS launch scale-up — the two launches carrying that 20% growth need country-level medical, field and patient-support operations that scale without adding headcount — which is the argument that survives a margin squeeze at home.
2Data operations behind the Owkin and Envisagenics deals — multimodal data governance, model validation and documentation. Both deals buy a platform; neither buys the operating discipline a regulator will ask about when an AI-identified target reaches the clinic.
3German market-access response — pricing and portfolio analytics for a 15.5% rebate environment, and the payer and policy communications behind investment decisions of the kind that just cost the German network €900M.

Risks to manage

■Sanofi — A formal EC antitrust investigation into campaign conduct makes every promotional claim and approval record discoverable. Keep proposals to governance, review and traceability — not campaign volume.
■CSL — After a US$2.6B loss, procurement scrutiny will be severe and slow. An unpriced capability proposal will not survive the first review, however well it is received by the business.
■Novartis — Two Phase III misses in one month means asset-level plans may be rebuilt. Confirm a programme is still funded before scoping launch work against it.
■Boehringer Ingelheim — The company has already cancelled €900M of German investment over pricing policy. German-market proposals need a margin case, not a growth case.
■Roche — A board nomination signalling commercial discipline alongside a portfolio this active points to vendor consolidation questions arriving with the launch work. Expect to defend scope as well as win it.
